title: Anthropic's Claude designs quantum circuits that beat the published state-of-the-art
subtitle: A STEM Fellows preprint pits an AI design loop against human-engineered benchmarks across eight computational tasks, and in seven of them Claude's circuits win on gate counts.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 15, 2026, researchers at Anthropic's STEM Fellows Program posted a preprint describing a closed-loop system in which Claude Mythos 5 designs quantum circuits against an automated evaluator. The paper, 'Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models' (arXiv:2610.22367), covers eight computational tasks spanning chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing. Claude receives a plain-language specification, proposes a circuit, and the evaluator scores it on correctness and cost — mainly by Toffoli-gate and qubit counts — and Claude then iterates on the feedback. Anthropic's own research page, titled 'Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude,' went up on October 16.

The headline figures matter because quantum resources are scarce. On seven of the eight benchmarks the discovered circuits reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art, with one point-addition design cutting gate count by roughly 17x at the cost of 12% more qubits, and a quantum decoder design using about 12x fewer gates. The eighth task produced a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion, a construction the authors describe as previously unpublished. Lead author Andi Gu worked with Anthropic's Alek Kemeny and physicists Susanne Yelin and Mikhail Lukin at Harvard, with QuEra Computing collaborating on the hardware side.

The result lands into a broader argument about where frontier LLMs can replace specialized symbolic tools. Code generation and theorem-proving have shown steady gains for a year, but quantum circuit design is harder — the correctness check is a quantum-simulation step, not a unit test, and the search space is combinatorial. The closed-loop framework matters more than any specific gate count: it is a template other labs can run on their own benchmarks and other kinds of discrete-optimization problems. The caveat is familiar for 2026 AI research — the paper is a preprint, the benchmarks were curated by its authors, and no independent group has reproduced the circuits yet.

Takeaway for learners: this is a worked example of an 'AI designs, AI judges' loop that produces something a human can verify. If you are learning to build with LLMs, the pattern is more portable than the quantum domain suggests — pair a generative step that proposes candidate solutions with a mechanical evaluator that scores them, and let the loop run. The scorer is where the honesty lives. A loop that cannot measure what it produces will produce impressive-looking garbage, so picking or building that scorer well is a bigger lever than picking a better model.
